chapters.title: Chapter 3: How Policy Flows Into Asset Prices

lessons.title: The Rupee, Forex Reserves, and RBI Intervention

body.text: The rupee is just another price, set by how many people want dollars versus rupees. The RBI does not defend a fixed level, but it refuses to let that price lurch. It smooths the ride by buying and selling from a war chest of foreign exchange reserves, and every one of those trades ripples back into Indian liquidity, interest rates and markets.

children.text: You have seen how the RBI's decisions flow into bonds and stocks. This lesson covers the third big market it shapes: the rupee. It explains what drives the currency, how the RBI intervenes, and what India's dramatic currency swings between 2024 and 2026 meant for investors, importers and anyone paying for something in dollars.
What Moves the Rupee
At its simplest, the rupee weakens when India needs more dollars than it receives, and strengthens when dollars pour in. The main flows are well known.

body.caption: Who Buys and Sells Dollars in India

cells: India imports most of its crude oil, so oil price spikes are a direct hit
Large and steady demand for dollars
One of India's biggest sources of dollar income
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances
Strengthens on inflows, weakens on outflows
Fast-moving money that reacts to global interest rates
Slower, longer-term money into factories and businesses

children.text: Where Interest Rates Come In

markDefs.definition: The difference between interest rates in two countries. A wider gap in India's favour attracts foreign investment into Indian bonds and supports the rupee.

children.text: Money flows to where it earns more, adjusted for risk. The gap between Indian and US interest rates, the
interest rate differential

, is a key driver of FPI flows into Indian bonds. When the RBI raises rates or the US Fed cuts, Indian bonds look more attractive and the rupee tends to firm. When the Fed hikes, money flows back to the US and the rupee weakens.

body.title: Measure the Rate Gap
body.prompt: In late August and early September 2026, the US 10-year Treasury yield was about 4.73% and India's 10-year G-Sec yield was about 6.96%. What is the interest rate differential in India's favour, in percentage points?
body.explanation: 6.96% minus 4.73% = 2.23 percentage points. That extra yield is what attracts foreign investors to Indian bonds. But they also bear currency risk: if the rupee falls more than about 2.2% in a year, a dollar-based investor loses money despite the higher yield. That is why rupee stability and interest rates are so closely linked.

children.text: How the RBI Manages the Rupee

markDefs.definition: An exchange rate system where the market sets the currency's value, but the central bank intervenes to smooth excessive volatility or disorderly moves.

children.text: Officially, India has a floating exchange rate: the market sets the rupee's value and the RBI does not target any level. In practice, the RBI runs a
managed float
: it steps in to stop sharp, disorderly moves while allowing the rupee to follow broader trends.

markDefs.definition: An IMF classification where a currency moves within a narrow band of about 2% around a steady trend for at least six months, reflecting heavy management rather than a free float.

children.text: The IMF watches what countries do, not just what they say. It reclassified India's de facto regime from floating to a "stabilised arrangement" in December 2023, and then in November 2025 to a
crawl-like arrangement
, meaning the rupee was moving along a narrow, predictable, gradually weakening path.

body.title: Free Float vs How the Rupee Is Actually Managed

columns.label: Free float
points: Market alone sets the price
Central bank rarely intervenes
Currency can swing sharply on news
Reserves needed only for emergencies

columns.label: India's managed approach
points: Market sets the trend, RBI smooths the path
Frequent intervention in spot and forward markets
IMF classed it as crawl-like in November 2025
Large reserves built up to absorb shocks

children.text: The War Chest: India's Forex Reserves

stats.label: Weekly jump
stats.context: The biggest weekly rise on record

body.title: Composition of India's Forex Reserves by Value, End-March 2026 (%)

markDefs.definition: Foreign currencies and highly liquid foreign securities, mainly US Treasury bonds, held by the RBI. They make up about 80% of India's reserves.

children.text: Most reserves are
foreign currency assets

, mostly held in safe, liquid instruments such as US Treasury bonds. Gold is the second-largest piece: the RBI held 880.52 tonnes at end-March 2026, and about 77% of it is now stored in India after large shipments home from the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements. Gold's share by value rose to 16.7% mainly because gold prices rallied, not because the RBI bought much more.

body.label: Import cover
body.context: In June 2026 the RBI Governor said reserves could pay for around 11 months of imports, a common measure of how safe a country's external position is.

children.text: How an Intervention Actually Works
The rupee starts falling sharply, say because oil prices jump and foreign investors sell.
The RBI, usually through public sector banks, sells dollars from its reserves in the spot market.
Banks buying those dollars pay the RBI in rupees, which adds supply of dollars and demand for rupees, slowing the fall.
Reserves go down, and the rupees paid to the RBI leave the banking system, tightening liquidity.
To offset that liquidity drain, the RBI may inject rupees back through OMO purchases, repo auctions or swaps.

markDefs.definition: Offsetting the effect of currency intervention on domestic money supply, for example by buying bonds to replace the rupee liquidity drained when the RBI sells dollars.

children.text: Step 5 has a name:
sterilisation

. It is why, as you saw in Chapter 2, a heavy rupee defence is so often followed by big OMO purchases and dollar swaps. The RBI can also intervene through forward contracts, promising to sell dollars at a future date, which supports the rupee today without spending reserves immediately.

body.title: Follow the Chain Reaction
body.question: The RBI sells $10 billion from its reserves to slow a falling rupee. Which set of effects is correct?
options: Reserves rise, bank liquidity rises, the rupee weakens
Reserves fall, bank liquidity falls, the rupee's decline slows
Reserves fall, bank liquidity rises, the rupee strengthens sharply
Reserves are unchanged, because the RBI prints the dollars
body.explanation: Selling dollars reduces reserves. Banks pay for those dollars in rupees, which leave the banking system, so liquidity tightens. The extra dollar supply slows the rupee's fall, though it rarely reverses a strong trend on its own. The RBI cannot print dollars; it can only spend the ones it has, which is why reserve levels matter.

children.text: Case 1: The Long Defence of 2024-25
Through late 2024 and early 2025, strong US dollar demand and heavy foreign selling put steady pressure on the rupee. The RBI fought back hard.

events.title: Reserves hit a record $704.89 billion
events.description: India entered the defence with its largest reserves ever at the time.

events.title: Heavy dollar sales
events.description: The RBI sold dollars in both spot and forward markets. Its net outstanding forward sales reached $88.7 billion by end-February 2025.

events.title: Reserves fall to $623.9 billion
events.description: Down more than 11% from the peak, while the liquidity drain pushed the banking system into deep deficit.

events.title: Rupee hits a then record low of 87.95
events.description: Despite the intervention, the rupee kept sliding, but in a controlled way rather than a crash.

body.title: How Much Did Reserves Fall?
body.prompt: India's reserves fell from $704.885 billion on 27 September 2024 to $623.9 billion on 17 January 2025. What was the percentage fall? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ($623.9 billion − $704.885 billion) ÷ $704.885 billion × 100 = -11.49%. Not all of that was intervention, since changes in the value of gold and other currencies also affect the total, but the bulk reflected the RBI selling dollars to smooth the rupee's fall.

body.text: The RBI did not stop the rupee from falling; it stopped it from falling fast. That is the heart of India's approach: accept the trend, fight the volatility. The rupee ended 2025 at 89.85 per dollar, about 5% weaker over the year, after briefly breaching 91 in December amid US trade tariffs and record foreign equity outflows.

children.text: Case 2: The Oil Shock and the Dollar Deluge, 2026

body.title: From Record Low to Record Reserves

events.title: Reserves at $723.77 billion
events.description: A new record, driven largely by a surge in the value of the RBI's gold as prices rallied.

events.title: West Asia conflict hits oil
events.description: Tensions involving Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz sent Brent crude close to $110 a barrel in May. Foreign investors pulled money out.

events.title: Rupee closes at a record low of 96.52
events.description: Down about 7% in 2026, making it Asia's worst-performing currency of the year.

events.title: Reserves down to $682.3 billion
events.description: The defence had cost over $40 billion from January's peak, including valuation changes.

events.title: FCNR(B) swap window
events.description: The RBI covered the hedging cost on fresh NRI foreign currency deposits. About $136 billion flowed in, including about $127 billion of FCNR(B) deposits.

events.title: Reserves hit $785.71 billion
events.description: A record, with the largest weekly jump ever. India overtook Russia to become the fourth-largest reserve holder.

body.title: India's Forex Reserves Through Two Defences ($ billion)
Rupees per US Dollar at Key Points (higher means a weaker rupee)

children.text: Notice the difference between the two defences. In 2024-25 the RBI mainly spent reserves. In 2026 it also found a way to attract new dollars, by making it cheap for banks to raise foreign currency deposits from NRIs. Reserves rebuilt to a record, yet the rupee was still near 95.6 per dollar in mid-September, because oil prices and global rate fears kept dollar demand high.

body.text: Record reserves built through swaps are not the same as reserves earned through trade surpluses. The FCNR(B) deposits and swaps mature in three to five years, when the dollars have to be returned. They buy India time and confidence, but they are borrowed strength.

children.text: Who Wins and Who Loses From a Weaker Rupee

body.title: The Two Sides of Rupee Depreciation

columns.label: Gain from a weaker rupee
points: IT services exporters such as TCS and Infosys, which earn in dollars
Pharma exporters such as Sun Pharma
Families receiving remittances from abroad
Indians holding US stocks or dollar assets

columns.label: Hurt by a weaker rupee
points: Oil marketing companies such as IOC, BPCL and HPCL, which buy crude in dollars
Companies with large unhedged dollar loans
Families paying for education or travel abroad
Consumers, as costlier imports feed inflation

body.title: What a Weaker Rupee Does to the Oil Bill
body.prompt: Brent crude is about $97 a barrel. At the end of 2025 the rupee was 89.85 per dollar; on 11 September 2026 it was about 95.6. At an unchanged oil price, how many more rupees does one barrel cost? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: At 89.85: $97 × 89.85 = ₹8,715. At 95.6: $97 × 95.6 = ₹9,273. Extra cost = about ₹558 a barrel, a 6.4% rise purely from the currency. Multiply that across millions of barrels a day and you can see why a weak rupee pushes up petrol, diesel and eventually overall inflation, which is exactly what the MPC worries about.

children.text: Economists describe a trade-off every country faces, called the impossible trinity. A country can choose only two of these three at the same time:
A fixed or tightly managed exchange rate
Free movement of capital in and out of the country
An independent monetary policy focused on domestic goals such as inflation

India keeps its monetary policy independent, with an inflation target, and has gradually opened its capital account. So it cannot also fix the rupee. Instead it manages volatility using reserves and accepts that the trend is set by the market. When the RBI intervenes heavily, it pays the price through liquidity drains that it must then sterilise, as the 2025 and 2026 episodes showed.

body.title: Paying US College Fees
body.scenario: Your cousin will pay $40,000 of US university fees in August 2027. It is September 2026: the rupee is at about 95.6 per dollar, having hit a record low of 96.52 in May. Reserves are at a record, but oil prices are high and the US Fed is considering rate hikes. Your cousin asks whether to buy dollars now or wait for the rupee to recover.
body.prompt: How should your cousin think about this decision? Is there a way to reduce the risk?
body.modelAnswer: Nobody can reliably forecast the rupee, including the RBI, which only aims to smooth volatility, not set a level. So the real question is how much uncertainty your cousin can afford. At 95.6, the fees cost about ₹38.24 lakh. If the rupee weakened another 5% to around 100, they would cost about ₹40 lakh, roughly ₹1.8 lakh more. If it recovered to 92, they would cost about ₹36.8 lakh. Over the past two years, the long-term trend has been a gradually weaker rupee, and a Fed hike or another oil spike could push it lower. A sensible middle path is to average in: convert part of the amount every month or quarter until the payment date, under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme or through an education loan disbursement plan. This avoids betting everything on one exchange rate. Waiting in the hope of a big recovery is a speculative bet on the currency, not a plan.

The IMF's November 2025 classification of the rupee: moving in a narrow band along a steady trend.
Foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and IMF reserve position held by the RBI. A record $785.71 billion on 4 September 2026.
How many months of imports reserves could pay for. About 11 months for India in 2026.
Offsetting the liquidity effect of currency intervention, for example through OMO purchases.
The gap between Indian and foreign interest rates, which drives foreign flows into Indian bonds.
A country cannot have a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and independent monetary policy all at once.

body.label: FBIL: Official Rupee Reference Rates
body.description: Financial Benchmarks India publishes the daily USD/INR reference rate used across Indian markets. Track it alongside the RBI's weekly Friday release of forex reserve data.

body.title: Track the Rupee Like a Treasury Desk
steps: Note today's USD/INR rate and compare it with the 2026 record low of 96.52
Find the latest weekly forex reserves figure, released by the RBI every Friday, and compare it with $785.71 billion
Check the current Brent crude price and think about what it means for India's import bill
Compare the US 10-year Treasury yield with India's 10-year G-Sec yield to estimate the rate gap
List any expenses you have in dollars, such as fees, travel or US investments, and note your exposure to a weaker rupee

points: The rupee is driven by the balance of dollar flows: oil and gold imports weaken it; exports, remittances and foreign investment strengthen it.
Interest rate gaps between India and the US drive foreign bond flows, so RBI and Fed decisions both move the rupee.
India officially floats the rupee, but the RBI manages volatility; the IMF classed the regime as crawl-like in November 2025.
Reserves hit a record $785.71 billion on 4 September 2026, about 80% foreign currency assets and 16.7% gold by value.
Selling dollars to defend the rupee drains rupee liquidity, which the RBI then offsets through sterilisation.
The rupee hit a record low of 96.52 in May 2026 despite heavy defence; record reserves from the FCNR(B) window bought stability, but with borrowed dollars.
